article.title: Why Revenue Growth Can Hide Customer Concentration Risk
article.why: 把 headline growth 與客戶集中風險分開評估。
article.author: OpenAI learning editor

paragraphs.en:
Revenue growth is usually treated as good news, but the source of that growth matters. A company can expand quickly while becoming more dependent on a small number of customers. If one or two large accounts explain most of the increase, headline growth can hide concentration risk.

Suppose a business grows revenue from 100 million to 125 million dollars. At first glance, 25 percent growth looks strong. But imagine that one customer increased spending from 8 million to 25 million. That single account explains most of the growth and now represents 20 percent of total revenue. If the customer leaves, delays a project, or negotiates harder, the impact will be much larger than it was before.

This is why analysts should look at both growth and distribution. Useful measures include the share of revenue from the largest customer, the top five customers, and the top ten. The trend is often more important than one fixed threshold. A top-customer share of 15 percent may be manageable if it is falling, but concerning if it rose from 5 percent in one year.

Contract quality also changes the risk. Twenty percent of revenue under a three-year committed contract is different from twenty percent under a short agreement that can be cancelled at any time. Renewal timing matters too. If several large contracts expire in the same quarter, concentration risk can become a timing risk.

Profitability is another layer. A large customer may generate impressive revenue but demand discounts, custom features, dedicated support, or special payment terms. In that case, revenue concentration may understate dependence because operational resources are even more concentrated than sales.

Concentration is not automatically bad. Large customers can provide stable volume, valuable references, and opportunities to expand into new products. The problem is unmanaged dependence. Management should know what would happen if a major account disappeared and how quickly the company could replace the lost revenue or reduce related costs.

Scenario analysis can make the risk concrete. Remove the largest customer from the forecast and recalculate revenue, gross profit, cash flow, staffing needs, and capacity utilization. Then ask whether the business could absorb the shock without emergency financing or severe restructuring.

A good growth report therefore separates two questions: how fast are we growing, and how diversified is that growth? The first question measures expansion. The second measures resilience.

This distinction is especially useful when evaluating sales teams. A team that wins one enormous contract may beat its annual target while building a fragile book of business. Another team may grow more slowly but add dozens of smaller accounts across industries. The second pattern may be more durable even if the headline growth rate is lower.

The main lesson is that growth quality matters. Revenue can rise while customer concentration, bargaining power, renewal risk, and cash-flow volatility all worsen. Strong analysis does not celebrate the numerator alone. It also asks how many independent relationships support it. Analysts should also distinguish customer concentration from sector concentration. Ten customers may look diversified, but if all ten depend on the same industry cycle, regulation, or commodity price, their risks can move together. Geographic concentration can create a similar problem. Diversification is therefore not only about the number of names; it is about whether the underlying sources of demand are genuinely independent.

Monitoring should be repeated over time. A dashboard can show top-customer share, top-five share, contract maturity, and concentration of gross profit. This makes deterioration visible before a renewal crisis occurs and helps management decide whether acquisition efforts should focus on smaller accounts, new segments, or longer commitments.
paragraphs.zh: 營收成長不代表風險一定下降。若新增收入主要來自少數大客戶，最大客戶或前五大客戶占比可能快速上升。除了營收占比，也要看契約期限、續約集中、毛利與專用支援成本，並做失去最大客戶的 scenario analysis。
paragraphs.ja: 売上成長が強くても、少数顧客への依存が高まれば事業は脆弱になります。最大顧客・上位5社の構成比、契約期間、更新時期、粗利や専用対応負荷まで確認し、主要顧客を失った場合のシナリオも見る必要があります。
